title: Trauma-Informed Lactation Care Following Perinatal Loss: A Scoping Review of Core Components of Care
abstract: Background: Lactation following perinatal loss is often an overlooked aspect of bereavement care. Mothers may experience physical discomfort alongside grief, emotional distress, changes in maternal identity, and decisions about lactation suppression, expression, or milk donation. Trauma-informed care may provide a framework for addressing these intersecting needs. Objectives: To map evidence on lactation care following perinatal loss and identify care components that can inform trauma-informed lactation practice. Methods: A scoping review was conducted to identify evidence on lactation experiences, management, and support following perinatal loss. Evidence was charted and inductively synthesized, followed by interpretation through a trauma-informed care lens. Results: A total of 26 peer-reviewed sources were included. Four interrelated core components were identified: (1) recognition, validation, and emotional safety; (2) maternal autonomy, choice, and individualized decision-making; (3) timely lactation information, education, and professional competence; and (4) integrated, continuous, and family-centred maternity and bereavement care. Lactation was experienced variably, ranging from physical and emotional distress to connection, maternal identity, meaning-making, and milk donation. Key gaps included inadequate anticipatory information, limited professional knowledge and confidence, inconsistent communication, fragmented care, and insufficient follow-up. Conclusions: Lactation following perinatal loss should be integrated into routine maternity and bereavement care rather than addressed solely as a physiological process requiring suppression. Trauma-informed care should prioritize emotional safety, maternal autonomy, timely and competent information, and coordinated continuity of care. Further research is needed to evaluate the implementation and effectiveness of these approaches.
